elements.id-string-3: Social disruption occurs when a policy creates or destroys many network connections between agents.
elements.id-string-4: It is a costly side effect of many interventions and so a growing empirical literature recommends measuring and accounting for social disruption when evaluating the welfare impact of a policy.
elements.id-string-5: However, there is currently little work characterizing what can actually be learned about social disruption from data in practice.
elements.id-string-6: In this paper, we consider the problem of identifying social disruption in a research design that is popular in the literature.
elements.id-string-7: We provide two sets of identification results.
elements.id-string-8: First, we show that social disruption is not generally point identified, but informative bounds can be constructed using the eigenvalues of the network adjacency matrices observed by the researcher.
elements.id-string-9: Second, we show that point identification follows from a theoretically motivated monotonicity condition, and we derive a closed form representation.
elements.id-string-10: We apply our methods in two empirical illustrations and find large policy effects that otherwise might be missed by alternatives in the literature.
elements.id-string-13: Many policies are socially disruptive in that they alter a substantial fraction of agents' social or economic connections.
elements.id-string-14: Since networks determine a wide range of economic activities, disrupting them can be harmful.
elements.id-string-15: For example, \cite{carrell2013natural} study a change in classroom composition that was supposed to improve academic performance but instead segregated students which exacerbated inequality.
elements.id-string-16: \cite{barnhardt2017moving} analyze an antipoverty program that was intended to provide economic opportunity but instead isolated participants which led to financial insecurity.
elements.id-string-17: Both policies were well intentioned but, because they were socially disruptive, ultimately hurt the agents that they were designed to help.\looseness=-1
elements.id-string-18: In light of these and other examples, a growing literature recommends measuring and accounting for social disruption when evaluating the welfare impact of a policy \citep[see, for instance,][]{banerjee2021changes,jackson2021inequality}.
elements.id-string-19: But identifying social disruption from data is not always straightforward in practice.
elements.id-string-20: Economists typically characterize the disruptive impact of a policy by comparing the average number of connections between agents with and without it.
elements.id-string-21: While easy to compute, comparing averages generally understates social disruption.
elements.id-string-22: The reason for this is that economic policies usually have heterogeneous effects: they create some connections and destroy others.
elements.id-string-23: If the amount of created connections is roughly the same as the amount of destroyed connections, then the average difference will be small, even when the total number of connections affected by the policy is not.\footnote{This disruption is policy relevant.
elements.id-string-24: It represents actual relationships that are upended, requiring time and resources to replace.
elements.id-string-25: The literature shows that new connections may be of lower quality, associated with less trust, communication, peer influence, etc.
elements.id-string-26: As a result, this disruption negatively impacts welfare, even when the average number of connections with and without the policy is similar.} \looseness=-1
elements.id-string-27: In this paper, we go beyond comparing averages and consider the problem of separately identifying the amount of connections created and the amount of connections destroyed by a policy.
elements.id-string-28: We focus on a research design that is popular in the literature.
elements.id-string-29: Agents are first randomly (or as good as randomly) assigned to one of two groups.
elements.id-string-30: The policy is implemented in one of the groups but not the other.
elements.id-string-31: The agents in each group then interact and report their connections.
elements.id-string-32: Versions of this design are considered, for example, by \cite{carrell2013natural,feigenberg2013economic,cai2015social,bajari2021multiple,banerjee2021changes,comola2021treatment,hess2021development,johari2022experimental}.
elements.id-string-33: Our first contribution is to propose a new framework to characterize the impact of a policy on the structure of a network in a randomized experiment.
elements.id-string-34: We do not specify an econometric model of link formation.
elements.id-string-35: Instead, we use the classical implication of random assignment, that the agents in the group subjected to the policy form connections that are in some sense representative of what the agents in the group not subjected to the policy would have realized had they been subjected to the policy.
elements.id-string-36: Formalizing this condition in the context of network data is not standard in econometrics, however, and our framework builds on ideas from the graph theory and operations research literatures \cite[see, generally,][]{lovasz2012large,cela2013quadratic}.
elements.id-string-37: Our second contribution is to derive two new sets of identification results.
elements.id-string-38: In the first set of results, we show that under no additional assumptions the amount of connections created or destroyed by a policy is partially identified.
elements.id-string-39: Sharp bounds on the identified set are given by a quadratic assignment problem (QAP), but these bounds are analytically and computationally intractable.
elements.id-string-40: Instead, we propose conservative outer bounds based on intersecting several relaxations of the QAP.
elements.id-string-41: These bounds are formed by simple rearrangements of the eigenvalues of the networks observed from the experiment, and so are straightforward to analyze and compute.
elements.id-string-42: In the second set of results, we give a sufficient condition for point identification.
elements.id-string-43: Our condition is a monotonicity assumption that is strong, but motivated from the network theory literature.
elements.id-string-44: Under this condition, the amount of social disruption is given by a difference in network eigenvalues that is also straightforward to analyze and compute.
elements.id-string-45: Though not the focus of our paper, sufficient conditions for consistent estimation and valid inference can be found in the online appendix.
elements.id-string-46: An R package for implementation can be found at \url{https://github.com/yong-cai/MatrixHTE}.
elements.id-string-47: We demonstrate our methodology with two empirical illustrations.

elements.id-string-49: Villages participate in a microfinance program and the network connections are informal risk sharing links between households.
elements.id-string-50: The authors compare the average number of connections between villages that do and do not participate and find that participation is associated with a one percent decrease in connections.

elements.id-string-186: This section describes our general framework.
elements.id-string-187: We focus on unipartite and undirected networks which are represented by symmetric adjacency matrices indexed by one population of agents.
elements.id-string-188: The framework and results immediately extend to asymmetric matrices or matrices indexed by two different populations under a standard symmetrization argument in Section 5.1.
elements.id-string-189: Our main results are in Section 4.
elements.id-string-191: A population of agents is indexed by the interval $[0,1]$.
elements.id-string-192: This choice of indexing set is arbitrary and the population may be finite or infinite.
elements.id-string-193: The population of agents may be assigned one of two policies, policy $0$ or policy $1$.
elements.id-string-194: Example policies include assigning every agent in the population to a treatment, assigning a random fraction of agents to a treatment, informing the entire population about the existence of a product, informing only community leaders about the existence of a product, etc.
elements.id-string-195: Our analysis does not depend on what the policy actually does, it only matters that the policy somehow determines the agents' network connections.
elements.id-string-196: Specifically, we focus on identifying the social disruption caused by changing the policy from policy $0$ to policy $1$ for the population of agents indexed by $[0,1]$.\looseness=-1
elements.id-string-197: Potential outcomes (network connections) are defined for every pair of agents and policy, and given by the measurable function $(Y^{*}_{1},Y^{*}_{0}):[0,1]^{2} \to \mathbb{R}^{2}$.
elements.id-string-198: In words, $Y_{t}^{*}(u,v)$ describes the connection between agents with indices $u$ and $v$ in the event that the population is assigned policy $t$.\footnote{This function is simply a definition of a matrix that allows for arbitrarily sized index sets.
elements.id-string-199: Any finite dimensional matrix can be represented by such a function, see Example 2 below, and it is analogous to representing a vector of data with its quantile function.
elements.id-string-200: This function is not an econometric model of network formation, nor does it impose any behavioral or functional form restrictions.} We take these potential outcomes to be fixed and bounded.
elements.id-string-201: Boundedness is straightforward but tedious to relax.
elements.id-string-202: Incorporating stochastic networks may be straightforward depending on the complexity of the statistical model chosen by the researcher.
elements.id-string-203: But since this complication is unrelated to our main identification results, we defer it to Online Appendix Sections D.4 where we discuss large sample estimation and inference.
elements.id-string-205: We do not rule out social spillovers, market forces, or other interactions between agents.
elements.id-string-206: Instead, we follow the literature and consider these interactions to be intermediate outcomes part of the policy effect of interest.
elements.id-string-207: While we could not find any examples of this in the network experiments literature, it is possible that a researcher could be interested in characterizing the impact of a change in policy under counterfactual interactions not observed in one of the treatment groups.
elements.id-string-208: For example, the researcher may be interested in alternative market equilibria that could have been but were not realized in the experiment.
elements.id-string-209: So long as the researcher is able to characterize the alternative equilibria using, for instance, a structural model, our methodology can be used to identify the relevant policy effect.

It focuses on a research design where agents are randomly (or as good as randomly) assigned to two groups. The policy of interest is implemented in one of the groups but not the other. Agents then interact and form connections. We first formalize the identifying content of randomization building on ideas from the graph theory and operations research literatures.
